title: Bezos-Backed CuspAI Raises $450 Million at $2.6 Billion Valuation to Discover New Chipmaking Materials
excerpt: The Cambridge-based startup uses AI to simulate and discover materials for semiconductors and clean energy, with ASML, Meta, and Nvidia among its early customers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • CuspAI raised $450 million, reaching a $2.6 billion valuation in just two years.
  • The startup uses AI to accelerate materials discovery for semiconductors and clean energy.
  • Notable customers include ASML, Meta, Hyundai, and Nvidia, part of its AI Materials Foundry.
  • CuspAI's advisory board includes AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun.
  • The company aims to reduce semiconductor manufacturing costs and reliance on rare materials.

  • CuspAI, a two-year-old Cambridge-based startup, has raised roughly $450 million at a $2.6 billion valuation, with Bezos Expeditions and Kleiner Perkins co-leading
  • The company uses AI to simulate and discover new materials for semiconductors, clean energy, and advanced manufacturing — cutting discovery timelines from decades to months
  • Its customers include chip equipment giant ASML, Meta, Hyundai, and Nvidia, who have joined its 'AI Materials Foundry' network
  • The startup's advisers include Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton and former Meta chief AI scientist Yann LeCun

CuspAI, a British startup that uses artificial intelligence to discover new materials for chipmaking and clean energy, has raised approximately $450 million in a round that values the company at $2.6 billion — more than five times its valuation from just nine months ago.

Bezos Expeditions, the investment vehicle of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, co-led the Series B alongside Silicon Valley venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins. Existing backers include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Northzone, NEA, and Temasek.

The fundraise represents one of the largest for a European AI startup this year and signals growing investor conviction that AI can meaningfully accelerate scientific discovery beyond software and language models.

A Search Engine for Materials

Founded in 2024 by Chad Edwards — who previously built quantum computing unicorn Cambridge Quantum — and Max Welling, a machine learning professor at the University of Amsterdam, CuspAI has built what it describes as a search engine for materials.

Its AI platform generates new molecular and atomic structures tailored to a customer's specifications, then tests them in digital simulations. Where traditional materials discovery requires years of laboratory trial and error, CuspAI claims to compress the process to months.

In April, the company open-sourced kUPS, a simulation toolkit that can speed up certain research tasks by a factor of 49. It has also demonstrated practical results: working with Finnish chemicals company Kemira, CuspAI explored 300 trillion possible molecular structures in six months to develop materials that could help remove "forever chemicals" from water. Kemira is now advancing 20 of those candidates.

Heavyweight Backers and Customers

CuspAI's advisory board features two of the most influential figures in AI research: Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun, Meta's former chief AI scientist and founder of world models startup AMI Labs.

The company's customer roster is equally notable. ASML, the Dutch firm whose lithography machines are essential to advanced chipmaking, is using CuspAI's platform alongside Meta, Hyundai, and Nvidia. These companies have joined CuspAI's recently launched "AI Materials Foundry," a global network aimed at accelerating breakthrough discoveries.

Why It Matters for the Chip Industry

Producing the world's most advanced semiconductors requires enormous energy and access to increasingly scarce minerals. As chip geometries shrink below 2 nanometres — the frontier where TSMC and Intel are competing — the industry faces mounting pressure to find new materials for conductors, insulators, and packaging that can withstand extreme heat and electrical demands.

CuspAI's approach could help address these bottlenecks. If AI can reliably identify materials that perform better than existing options, it could reduce the semiconductor industry's dependence on rare elements and lower manufacturing costs — factors that would benefit chip fabs globally, including India's ambitious $13.3 billion semiconductor package that is funding new facilities by Tata and Micron.

The company's rapid valuation growth — from $520 million last September to $2.6 billion today — places it among Europe's fastest-growing AI startups. It topped Sifted's AI 100 ranking last year as the most promising AI startup valued at under $1 billion, a threshold it has now cleared five times over.
